title: MA9-01574
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, the principal claimant, her adult children, XXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and her minor son, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXX, who are Mexican citizens, are claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The principal claimant was appointed the designated representative for her minor child. The children are basing their claims on their mother's claim.
The panel took into consideration the Chairperson's guideline entitled Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution, pursuant to paragraph 159(1)(h) of the IRPA.

The principal claimant is afraid of XXXXXX, who threatened the members of her family. Those people had been searching for the principal claimant's spouse, XXXXXXXXXXXX, who was in Canada at the time. The persecutors, XXXXXX, had been unable to locate Mr. XXXXXXXX, and so they targeted his family as a way of finding him. Consequently, if they are forced to return to Mexico, the principal claimant and her three children would once again be targeted by those individuals, who had it in for Mr. XXXXXXXX.

The decision in the refugee protection claim of the principal claimant's spouse, XXXXXXXX XXXX, was rendered on April 28, 2011, by XXXXXXXXXX. She found that Mr. XXXXXXX was a person described in Article 1F(b) of the Convention, because he had been found in his car with XXXXX g of marijuana in his possession. In this case, and subject to sections 4 and 5, trafficking and possession of marijuana in an amount exceeding three kilograms for the purpose of trafficking is an offence punishable by a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Mr. XXXXXXX was arrested in XXX 2000. The panel did not believe his explanations and attached more probative value to the information contained in the ruling that found him guilty.

According to the principal claimant's initial Personal Information Form (PIF), her problems began on XXXXXXX, 2008, at around 6:30 p.m., when she received a telephone call and was asked where her husband was. That same day, the principal claimant telephoned her husband, XXXXXXXX XXXXX, who was living in Montréal, and he told her to say nothing, because no one was to know where he was living.

On XXXXXXXX, 2008, the same person telephoned the principal claimant and again asked for her husband's whereabouts. Having received no reply other than that Mr. XXXXXXXX was no longer living there, the caller became angry with the principal claimant and insulted and threatened her, saying that she and her children might have a serious accident. He also stated he knew everything about her and her children, and he told her not to attempt to obtain the police's help, or she would regret it.

The principal claimant again telephoned her husband in Canada, and Mr. XXXXXXXX told her that she and the children had to leave the house and go into hiding at the home of a brother, XXX. Mr. XXXXXXXX added that he would look whether it would be possible for them to come to Canada.

The next day, XXXXXXXX, 2008, the principal claimant and her children went to live at XXXX house in the city of XXXXXXX, in the state of Morelos. That same day, Mr. XXXXXXXX telephoned to say that the principal claimant and her children could travel to Canada, and that is why the principal claimant quickly took steps to obtain passports and buy the tickets.

Because her son XXXX accidentally got his passport wet on XXXXX, 2008, the claimants had to make new arrangements to obtain this travel document. On XXXXXX, 2008, the principal claimant purchased airplane tickets to Canada. The claimants all travelled on XXXXXXXX, 2008, and filed refugee protection claims upon their arrival at the Trudeau airport that same day.

Significant additions were made to the PIFs on May 26, 2011. The principal claimant added that sometime around XXXXXXXX, at around 5:00 a.m., someone knocked at their door and her son opened it. Individuals entered their home and pointed a gun, asking to see the principal claimant's husband. She was beaten, and her children were terrified and screamed. Some neighbours came over. The assailants told the principal claimant that that would not save her, and they again ordered her not to contact the police, or they would kill her and her children.

A second change to the narrative was submitted on May 6, 2011, when the principal claimant added, in the last four paragraphs, that she had suffered physical and psychological abuse at the hands of her husband. The principal claimant stated that she had filed a complaint in Mexico with the DIF, which suggested that she go and file a complaint with the police. She had refused to pursue this course of action any further. She was still hoping to change the situation with the help of therapy. Her husband did not appear when notified by the authorities, and the latter had told the principal claimant that her husband would be arrested if he did not appear. In Canada, the principal claimant found the courage to leave her husband. XXXX was arrested for spousal abuse and released on bail on XXXXXXX, 2011. His trial hearing is scheduled for XXXXXXX, 2012. ANALYSIS Identity
The identity of the claimants was established to the panel's satisfaction by means of photocopies of their Mexican passports. Determinative issues
The determinative issues are credibility and state protection. Credibility
At the start of the hearing, the principal claimant confirmed that the entire content of the PIF was complete, true and correct.

The principal claimant was asked to explain the omission in the amendment received on May 6, 2011, of the events that allegedly happened on XXXXXXXX, 2008. On this date, some men allegedly came to the door, and her son XXXXXXX let them in. The men-who were armed-pulled the principal claimant's hair, beat her and ordered her to tell them the whereabouts of her husband. Also added was the fact that the principal claimant's children supposedly saw her bleeding and started to scream desperately, even though one of the men had allegedly told them to be quiet or he would shoot them. The men apparently kept pressing her to find out where XXXX was. When asked to explain why all these important facts were omitted, the principal claimant blamed Mr. XXXX assistant, XXXXXXXXXX. When asked whether she had kept a copy of the original Spanish version of the PIF, the principal claimant stated that it was not in writing. The panel notes that this amendment was produced approximately eight days after the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) decision's concerning XXXXXXXXXXX was rendered. The panel does not accept that blaming Ms. XXXXXX constitutes an explanation. This undermines the principal claimant's credibility on this aspect of her testimony.

Significant additions were also made to the PIF on May 26, 2011: the principal claimant mentioned that XXXX was a heavy drinker and that he used to beat her. The principal claimant added that when XXXX went to prison, the principal claimant's brother allegedly invited her to a group meeting where she talked about matters related to spousal abuse.

The principal claimant testified that one day, XXXX beat her and she decided to leave him. She allegedly left and rented a house with the children, but four months later, she returned to live with XXXX. Things apparently calmed down with XXXX, but this was after they had the problems related to XXXX kidnapping.

The principal claimant did not mention spousal abuse in the initial PIF. The panel is of the opinion that this fact was added to embellish her story. This undermines the principal claimant's credibility on this aspect of her testimony.

The principal claimant spoke of a death threat made on XXXXXXXXX, 2008, when the persecutors supposedly told her that they had confined XXXX and that he had escaped that night. When asked why this fact was omitted in the narrative, the principal claimant replied: [translation] "I didn't say it, I was under a lot of stress." The panel does not accept that explanation. This undermines the principal claimant's credibility on this aspect of her testimony.
In short, the panel does not believe the principal claimant or her story. State protection
Even if the principal claimant were credible, the issue of state protection remains.

Except in situations of complete breakdown of the state apparatus, it should be assumed that the state is capable of protecting its citizens.1 The presumption that the state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a claimant has no other recourse available.2

To rebut the presumption of state protection, a refugee protection claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.3 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, but must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.4 In this case, the panel is not satisfied on a balance of probabilities.

The burden of proof on the claimant is directly proportional to the level of the democracy in the state in question. The more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to him.5

The refugee protection claimant must demonstrate that he has taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.6

In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection within the country of origin will usually be fatal to a refugee claim-at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.7
In this case, the principal claimant did not file a complaint with the police, either orally or in writing. The reason she gave was the fact that she was afraid.

The DIF, the state's public agency providing family services to which the principal claimant turned, asked her whether she wanted to initiate legal proceedings. The principal claimant did not want to go take such action, although she did undergo therapy once or twice. She explained: [translation] "I no longer trust the authorities."

The adequacy of state protection cannot rest on a claimant's subjective fear.8 A refugee protection claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy simply by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state in providing protection.9 No state can guarantee perfect protection.10 Adequate protection is the standard to be satisfied.

The panel has reviewed the reasons for the persuasive decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) in file number TA6-07453, dated November 26, 2007, and adopts its line of reasoning on the availability of state protection.
The principal claimant has not rebutted the presumption of state protection in the circumstances of this case.
The panel determines that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX are neither "Convention refugees" nor "persons in need of protection."

Their claim for refugee protection is rejected.
